title: Stability of Quantum LDPC States under Local Pauli Noise
authors: Tai-Hsuan Yang, Andrew D. Kim, Akash Vijay, Jong Yeon Lee
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have a canonical mixed state---the normalized projector onto the code space---that lies at the intersection of quantum error correction and quantum many-body physics, yet the stability of its information-theoretic structure under local noise remains poorly understood. Recent progress on mixed-state phases of matter has identified the spatial decay of conditional mutual information (CMI) $I(A:C|B)$ as a key diagnostic of such stability, analogous to the role of the spectral gap for quantum ground states. We prove that, for the normalized code-projector state of a $\mathbb{Z}_d$ qLDPC stabilizer code under local Pauli noise, the CMI across a buffer $B$ separating $A$ from $C$ decays exponentially with the width of $B$ in two complementary noise regimes independent of system size. At weak noise, this holds for full-system tripartitions, where correlations between the two sides require an error cluster to cross the buffer, an exponentially unlikely event. At strong noise, exponential decay holds whenever the buffer supports no logical operator, since correlations can persist only along rare chains of buffer qudits that remain informative. Under an additional space-uniformity assumption, we establish the robustness of Levin--Wen topological entropy. On finite-dimensional lattices of size $n$, the weak-noise bound further implies a constant-layer quasi-local Petz recovery channel of range $O(\poly(\log n)/\varepsilon)$ that recovers the noiseless state within trace-distance error $\varepsilon$. Both CMI bounds apply to general qLDPC interaction graphs, including geometries where such constant-depth quasi-local recovery need not exist. Thus, the exponential decay of the noise-induced CMI provides a general criterion for mixed-state phase stability.
summary: This work establishes a general criterion for the stability of quantum error-correcting codes by analyzing the decay of the Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) under local Pauli noise. The authors prove exponential decay of CMI across any separating region in both weak and strong noise limits. This result is significant because it provides a robust, quantifiable measure of information preservation in complex quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the stability of the canonical mixed state of Quantum LDPC codes under local Pauli noise.
main_result: It proves that the Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) decays exponentially with the width of any separating buffer in both weak and strong noise regimes.
method: The analysis uses the CMI as a diagnostic tool, deriving bounds through techniques analogous to error-cluster arguments and information-percolation inequalities.
model_or_system: The system is based on Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) codes defined on a lattice, whose canonical mixed state is the normalized projector onto the code space. Noise is modeled by local Pauli channels.
key_observables: Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), $I(A:C|B)$, and the exponential decay rate of this quantity.
important_parameters: Noise strength ($p$), system size ($n$), and the separation distance across the buffer ($B$).
main_assumptions: The results are rigorously established for full-system tripartitions, and some parts require additional assumptions like space-uniformity or local-normalizer completeness.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate CMI partitions ($A \sqcup B \sqcup C$), show the rigorous exponential CMI decay for the Toric Code under X-dephasing, and depict the geometry of deformations and the Petz recovery map construction.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the CMI decay bound in two complementary regimes (weak and strong noise) using different mathematical tools, and concludes by applying these bounds to construct a quasi-local Petz recovery channel.
why_interesting: The use of CMI decay as a general, quantifiable criterion for mixed-state phase stability provides a powerful tool applicable beyond standard ground-state gap arguments in quantum many-body physics.
